title: Transfer: House Robber on a Circular Street
oneLiner: Same no-two-neighbours rule, but the houses form a circle. Break the circle into two straight streets and reuse the linear answer.
keyTakeaway: When a changed requirement adds one constraint that couples the ends, split on it: either the first house is skipped or the last one is (both can't be robbed). Each case is the original linear problem on a shorter range, so the answer is the max of two runs of code you already have.
explanation:
This follows House Robber with one requirement changed: the houses stand in a circle, so house 0 and house n - 1 are neighbours too. Return the most you can collect without robbing two neighbours. For [2, 3, 2] the answer is 3: robbing both 2s is no longer allowed, because they are neighbours.

Running the linear recurrence once is wrong, since it may pick both ends. Trying to patch the recurrence with a flag ("did I rob house 0?") works but is easy to get wrong. The cleaner move is to split on the new constraint. In any valid choice, at least one of house 0 and house n - 1 is skipped. If house 0 is skipped, the rest, houses 1 to n - 1, is an ordinary straight street; if house n - 1 is skipped, houses 0 to n - 2 are. Every valid circular choice is a valid choice in one of the two straight streets, and every choice in either straight street is valid on the circle, so the answer is the larger of the two linear answers.

Write the linear solver once as a helper that takes a range (start and end index) and use the same two rolling variables as before: cur = max(prev1, prev2 + nums[i]). Watch the small cases: no houses gives 0, and a single house has no neighbour at all, so the answer is its value (both ranges would be empty otherwise). Two linear passes, O(n) time and O(1) space.

The visualization runs [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] as a circle: first the street without the last house, then the street without the first house.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences on why the two straight streets cover every valid circular choice and nothing invalid. Then name another problem where a constraint joining the two ends could be handled the same way, by splitting into cases that each reduce to a problem you already solved.

recognitionSignals: A known linear DP, but the sequence is circular: the first and last items now interact.
A constraint that couples two specific positions, which you can remove by splitting into a small number of cases.
gotchas: One house: return its value. Excluding the first or the last house would leave nothing.
The two ranges are 0..n-2 and 1..n-1, both inclusive. Off by one here silently drops a house.
Running the linear version on the whole array can rob both ends: [2, 3, 2] would give 4 instead of 3.
confusableWith: 1-D DP: House Robber is the same recurrence on a straight street; this version only adds the case split around it.

complexity.note: Two linear House Robber passes over n - 1 houses each, with two rolling variables per pass.
